task_row_model.query: For a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials assessing a behavioral weight-loss intervention versus control, what minimal eligibility criteria should be applied and which effect size metric should be used?

documents.content: Methods: Trials eligible for pooled analysis were randomized, parallel-group studies of behavioral weight-loss interventions delivered to adults (age ≥18). Comparators included usual care, minimal intervention, or no-treatment/waitlist controls. We required at least 12 weeks' follow-up to capture sustained weight change. Primary outcome was change in body weight reported in kilograms; analyses depended on reported summary statistics (mean and SD for change or endpoint). When all trials reported weight in the same units (kg), the pooled effect was calculated as a mean difference; the study recommended a standardized mean difference only when outcomes used different metrics (e.g., BMI or percent weight) and could not be converted.
documents.reasoning_trace: Contains key eligibility items (randomized parallel-group, adults ≥18, comparators, ≥12 weeks), outcome preference (weight in kg with mean and SD), and guidance to use mean difference when same units and SMD when metrics differ.

documents.content: Background guidance often permits combining change-from-baseline or post-intervention endpoint weights provided they are on the same scale and comparable across trials. Reviews usually require usable dispersions (SD, SE, or 95% CI) for mean differences; if only medians or ranges are reported authors may be contacted or conversion formulas applied. Trials reporting weight as percent change or BMI are considered for pooling only if convertible to absolute kilograms; otherwise a standardized mean difference is used to synthesize heterogeneous scales. This section also reiterates excluding non-randomized designs and ensuring unit consistency before choosing the effect measure.
documents.reasoning_trace: Specifies that change-from-baseline or endpoint are acceptable if same scale, need for SDs, and when to convert or use SMD for non-convertible metrics.

documents.content: Researcher's note: I exclude crossover and unadjusted cluster trials unless they present appropriately adjusted effect estimates. Comparator labels vary—'usual care' can be minimal counselling or no contact—so eligibility should prespecify acceptable control types. Minimum follow-up of roughly three months is practical for behavioural interventions to avoid transient effects. Practical inclusion also depends on reporting of means and SDs for weight; without them, trial data are unusable for a mean-difference meta-analysis unless reconstructed from other reported statistics.
documents.reasoning_trace: Adds exclusion of crossover/unadjusted cluster trials, clarifies comparator heterogeneity, reiterates ~12-week minimum follow-up and requirement for means/SDs for MD pooling.

documents.content: News feature: Rising obesity rates have prompted a range of behaviour-change programmes worldwide. Journalists often highlight individual success stories and policy debates rather than methodological details. While commentators speculate on long-term maintenance, these pieces rarely report trial-level summary statistics like means and standard deviations needed for meta-analysis; they instead quote percentage reductions or participant anecdotes, which are not directly usable for quantitative pooling without conversion or further data.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides noise: emphasizes lack of usable trial statistics in media reports and is a source of tangential commentary, not methodological guidance.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Include randomized, parallel-group trials in adults (≥18) of behavioral weight‑loss interventions versus usual care/minimal or no‑treatment controls, with at least 12 weeks (≈3 months) follow‑up and reported means and SDs for weight (change-from-baseline or endpoint) in kilograms. Pool as mean difference when all trials report kg on the same scale; use standardized mean difference only if outcomes use non-convertible different metrics (e.g., BMI or percent weight). Exclude crossover or unadjusted cluster trials unless appropriately adjusted.
